sources.headline: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
sources.text: Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal, which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.A sign in Shenzen’s business district promoting the Apec summit. Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPASome analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine, which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.That is believed to be unpalatable to China, which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionAnalysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum. “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

President Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.Mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence.For Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports.Echoes of YaltaThe highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China.The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. sources.headline: Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
sources.text:
U.S. President Trump attends a ceremony in honor of Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery on Nov. 11 in Arlington, Va.
Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
hide caption
Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit. The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year, and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections, potentially weakening his bargaining position across the Pacific. The president and administration officials – including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – are also under scrutiny after the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
Huang traveled to China with Trump earlier this year – this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen. The expectation for major deals or pronouncements coming out of the meetings this week are low – but the meeting is still expected to make waves over the imagery of the trilateral summit. Trump said as he left the White House Monday that he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines where he'll meet with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila. The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days. Trilateral meeting For weeks the president has said he's keen to discuss the Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. But Edgard Kagan, the former ambassador to Malaysia and a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said it's a topic that Xi likely won't want to get into. The White House confirmed Friday that Trump is expected to meet with Xi and Putin together. "The Chinese strongly disagree with the idea that they should be involved in any kind of trilateral discussions with the United States and Russia on nuclear weapons," Kagan said.
"China wants to avoid this because they don't want to be locked into a subservient position. And they also don't want to create a precedent. I think the main thing for the Chinese is they know if they do a meeting and nuclear issues are discussed, it becomes much harder for them to refuse to do it in the future," he said. A White House official said they do not expect any agreement to come out of the meeting on denuclearization. "We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said, calling the trilateral an "entry point" for the three countries to talk about reducing nuclear weapons stock. Another U.S. official not authorized to speak on the record acknowledged that denuclearization is a "difficult" topic for China. "But we do think it's time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official said. Putin, for his part, stands to benefit from a meeting with Trump and Xi, as Russia's war with Ukraine nears its five-year mark. Trump has made friendlier moves toward Russia in recent months, siding with Putin and striking a deal to release more Russian oil into the market ahead of the midterm elections. Trump said last month that he was fine with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy not being present at a potential meeting with Putin about the war. "Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said. A White House official said Ukraine is not intended to come up in the meeting with Xi and Putin. And there is no plan for Putin and Trump to have a separate meeting. But Trump said Monday he would be talking about his "favorite subject Ukraine."
Kagan said the meeting with Xi, Trump and Putin could end up being on the shorter side if there isn't much all parties are willing to discuss. But at the same time, "I could see this going longer because President Trump likes dealing with Putin and Xi. He sees them as his peers. He sees them as important world leaders," Kagan said. Either way, a photo of the three leaders meeting together is enough to make headlines. "That picture alone is going to be worth well over a thousand words," Kagan said. Busan Agreement This is the second time Trump and Xi are meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit – but this year's meeting is notably different from last year's in Busan, South Korea, when tensions between the US and China were fraught amid the escalating trade war. The meeting in Busan established a sort-of truce between the two countries. The U.S. immediately lowered some tariffs on Chinese goods and China agreed to loosen exports on rare earths. But the execution of the agreement has been spotty. "There's friction in this truce. It's not smooth, but it's basically functional," Kurt Tong, Managing Partner at The Asia Group, said. A White House official said the U.S. isn't getting rare earths from China at the pace or level they'd like. "We really want to focus minds among our counterparts in China on compliance with this," they said. Still, Tong expects the agreement to be renewed past its January expiration. The two sides will likely agree to the renewal either in Shenzhen or later this year at the G20 summit Trump is hosting in Miami, according to Tong. Meetings in Manila Before the president arrives in China, he's holding meetings with several allies in Manila, including a meeting with the other leaders of the Quad nations: India, Japan and Australia.
"I think it's quite significant symbolically and politically that the U.S., Australia, Japan and India, the major democracies of Asia and the Pacific, get together… it's especially significant that they're doing it just before the meetings in China," Tong said. The White House said Trump will also sign a trade deal with Thailand while in the Philippines. The opportunity in Manila for Trump is to repair and reinforce relationships with countries like Japan and India, and the host country the Philippines. The ASEAN summit is also the region's first look at the president since his party lost control of Congress and on a global stage, a chance to see what the last two years of Trump's presidency may look like. "I think the real thing that people will be looking at first is, how does he present himself?" Kagan said. "How does his behaviour towards Modi and towards India change? Those are things people will be looking at very, very closely for clues for what the next two years are likely to be like." Nvidia fallout A White House official said they don't expect Trump to raise the issue of Huang's affair and resignation with Xi. The focus of the meeting is about trade, the official said. Huang resigned last week after admitting the extramarital affair with Alice Huang. Trump administration officials are now facing scrutiny and questions about how much they knew about Huang's affair and how much Huang had access to Trump and his orbit. Trump reiterated Monday he wasn't sure if Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and that he wouldn't mind seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia's CEO. "I think the main impact is here in the United States, where there are calls for accountability with respect to Mr. Huang's activities with the U.S. government and questions about what happened… the net result of that is to provide a tailwind to persons who are interested in tightening up the technology denial regime toward China," Tong said.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed last week to appear in front of the Senate Banking Committee to answer further questions. Trump stood by Lutnik on Monday, saying there were differing views on how to treat China in his administration.

South Korea fears that nuclear arms talks this week between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts could undermine efforts to denuclearise North Korea, potentially leaving Seoul sidelined in decisions affecting its own security.

Analysts and South Korean officials have expressed concern that the talks may treat the North as an established nuclear power, weakening international pressure on Pyongyang to give up its weapons in favour of efforts to limit its arsenal.

The planned meeting between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin on Thursday has also revived memories in Seoul of the 1945 Yalta Conference, where great-power diplomacy helped shape the post-World War II order and set the stage for the eventual division of the Korean peninsula.

“South Korea is worried that the tripartite summit could be a repetition of the Yalta Conference, where major powers reshaped the world order without consulting countries such as Korea that were directly affected by their decisions,” Koh Yu-hwan, an emeritus professor at Dongguk University, told This Week in Asia.

South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun (left) with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing on Friday. Photo: Xinhua

On Saturday, a senior South Korean foreign ministry official said he had raised concerns about the US-China-Russia summit’s potential implications for Seoul during separate meetings with his American and Chinese counterparts.

“I explicitly told my Chinese counterpart that the US-China-Russia summit should not become another Yalta Conference,” the official said on condition of anonymity.

“We have emphasised that no decisions should be made – such as recognising North Korea as a nuclear-armed state or undermining efforts to establish a peace regime – that would run counter to our government’s objectives, and China understood this well.”

Last Friday, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing, stressing that “the Korean peninsula issue is a matter of vital interest to us”.

The original Yalta Conference was held in February 1945, bringing together the leaders of the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union.

The three powers at the time discussed placing Korea, then under Japanese colonial rule, under a multilateral trusteeship before it gained full independence following Japan’s defeat.

Korea, however, had little say in the later division of the peninsula that saw the South placed under US military administration and the North under Soviet military rule.

For Seoul, the concern goes beyond the prospect of another Yalta-style agreement. Even without a formal deal, discussions that shift the focus from eliminating North Korea’s nuclear weapons to managing its arsenal could weaken the long-standing international commitment to denuclearisation.

Trump has made clear that he intends to discuss reducing nuclear weapons worldwide, arguing that their proliferation is “very dangerous”, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales has said.

Iran is also understood to be on the agenda, while Ukraine is not expected to feature prominently.

No agreement is expected to emerge from the talks, an unnamed senior US official was reportedly quoted as saying.

01:51
North Korea’s Kim attends live-fire drone and rocket demonstration in Wonsan

Koh said the Korean peninsula issue was likely to take a back seat to the major powers’ immediate strategic priorities.

“But Seoul is concerned that its security interests could become subject to Trump’s transactional diplomacy, potentially reinforcing North Korea’s narrative that its nuclear weapons are necessary to defend itself against hostile forces,” he said.

Cha Du-hyeogn, a senior research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, warned that China and Russia could use discussions on nuclear arms reduction to reinforce Pyongyang’s argument that its weapons were defensive and necessary to counter US hostility.

The concern is particularly acute because South Korea has traditionally taken part in multilateral negotiations over the North’s nuclear programme, but would have no seat at the trilateral summit.

Seoul’s unease has also been fuelled by signs that Beijing and Moscow are increasingly emphasising political negotiations rather than dismantling Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal.

In a joint statement issued after their summit in May, Xi and Putin merely called for a “political solution” to issues surrounding the Korean peninsula, and voiced opposition to diplomatic isolation, economic sanctions and military pressure on North Korea.

For Seoul, the worry is that any shift towards accepting North Korea’s nuclear arsenal could influence Washington’s approach and make it easier for Trump to pursue a separate deal with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that limits or freezes his nuclear programme, rather than requiring its dismantlement.

Kurt Campbell, a former US deputy secretary of state, said last week that North Korea’s apparent demand for recognition as a nuclear power could complicate Trump’s efforts to arrange another summit with Kim.

“My understanding, at least, is that the North Koreans have communicated to the United States that the only condition under which there could be consideration for a summit is if the United States accepted North Korea as a nuclear power,” Campbell said during a press briefing hosted by the Asia Group.

“Given the current circumstances, I think that would be almost impossible for President Trump to accept,” he said, noting that such a move could face opposition from both Republicans and Democrats in Congress.

Cha similarly saw little prospect of an early Trump-Kim summit, saying negotiations with Pyongyang were likely to rank below the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine on Trump’s list of priorities.

“Even if President Trump harbours a personal fondness for Kim and maintains an interest in negotiations, he must weigh what could realistically be gained from a US-North Korea summit,” Cha said.

North Korea’s leader Kim Jong-un (right) with US President Donald Trump in the Joint Security Area of Panmunjom in the demilitarised zone on June 30, 2019. Photo: AFP

Unlike in 2018 and 2019, a meeting with Kim could no longer be touted as an achievement in itself, and North Korea was likely to demand a much higher price for returning to negotiations, he added.

Cha also warned that any deal effectively condoning North Korea’s nuclear arsenal could provoke backlash, particularly given Trump’s hardline stance towards Iran over its nuclear ambitions.

He said there was a remote possibility that Trump could pursue what he described as a “bad deal” with Pyongyang, but believed an early summit was unlikely.

The possibility of Washington shifting from denuclearisation to negotiating limits on North Korea’s arsenal has meanwhile prompted warnings in the South Korean media.

In an editorial published on Monday, the Korea JoongAng Daily urged Seoul to secure a firm commitment from Washington that future negotiations with Pyongyang “will not replace denuclearisation with a nuclear freeze or arms control arrangement”.

“The South cannot afford to become a bargaining chip in negotiations among nuclear powers. It must directly represent and protect its security interests throughout the diplomatic process,” it added.

The Korea Times argued on Sunday that South Korea “has both the standing and the means to make its voice heard” and its future “will be determined by the choices it makes today, not by agreements or treaties struck by other countries behind its back”.

Park Chan-kyong

sources.headline: Trump heads to Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
sources.text:
By
Updated on: November 16, 2026 / 7:45 PM EST
/ CBS News
Add CBS News on Google
Washington — President Trump is setting off Monday for a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week. Ahead of his departure, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China. The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first between the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed. The president will first head to the Philippines, where the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is being held. Mr. Trump will meet with Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said. On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi.Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce."I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking. Mr. Trump is not expected to speak about the 4 ½-year war in Ukraine during the summit.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip."We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job. Both Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips. Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.
